## Part 1: Analysis of Study data

# Introducion

This CP requires to install three R packages. In R-Studio this can be done through the menu or in the console with:

```{r}
    #install.packages(c('lme4', 'reshape2', 'ggplot2'))
```

The data is contained in file `lxw.rds` and contains tumor size measurements (surface area) for several mice (`mousenr`) coming from two strains (`group`). Size measurements can be found in columns `lxw*`.

# Learning R

Load the data set `lxw.rds` and show the data by typing `d` in the console.

```{r}
    d <- readRDS('data/lxw.rds')
```

This data set contains all measurements for each mouse in a single row (wide format). To analyze the data, these measurements have to be put into separate rows (long format). Package `reshape2` contains functions to change a data set between long and wide format.

The function `melt` changes from wide into long format.

```{r}
    library('reshape2')
    dLong <- melt(d, c('mousenr', 'group'), c('lxw0', 'lxw2', 'lxw4', 'lxw6'), variable.name = 'time', value.name = 'tsize')
    dLong
```
The first argument is the data set in wide format. The second argument are so-called `id.vars`, which identify the units (mice) in the data. Values of these variables are repeated for each measurement in the output data `dLong`. The third argument contains the repeated measurements on the unit (mouse). For each of these columns, a new row is created in the output data per unit. The final arguments determing column names in the output data.

Check `dLong` and make sure you understand how it relates to the original data `d`.

A data set in long format can be converted back to wide format using function `dcast`.

```{r}
    d1 <- dcast(dLong, mousenr + group ~ time)
```

This function takes two arguments: the data in long format and a formula of the form `id.vars1 + idvars2 + ... ~ measruement`. The variables on the left hand side are again the identifying variables and the right hand variable is the variable identifying the measurement. The remaining variables are put into separate columns.

Check that `d` and `d1` are identical.

Create a plot using `ggplot2` which shows all measurements. Connect measurements of each mouse with a line and use a color for the group (the so-called the spaghetti plot of the data): `ggplot(dLong, aes(x = time, y = tsize, color = group, group = mousenr)) + geom_line() + geom_point()`.

Create a plot showing the mean and standard deviation per group/time point. This is called the mean profile plot.

Use the `by` and `mnSe` functions as in the linear regression CP to make the calculations per sub-group.

```{r}
    se <- function(x) sd(x)/sqrt(length(x))
    mnSe <- function(d) c( d[1, c('group', 'time')], mean=mean(d$tsize), se=se(d$tsize) )
    meanSe <- by(dLong, dLong[, c('group', 'time')], mnSe)
```

The function `mnSe` computes mean and standard error (SE) of column `tsize`. It also returns the combination of values for which mean/SE were computed.
In this case, the second argument to `by` is the reduced data frame with only columns `group` and `time`. The `by` function iterates through all combinations of values found in these to columns and calls `mnSe` with the sub-data frames.

Use the following line to create a data frame from the result. You can use it as a fixed recipe or look up the functions `lapply`, `do.call`, `as.data.frame`, and `unlist` yourself.

```{r}
    dMnSe <- as.data.frame(lapply(as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, meanSe)), unlist))
```

Create the mean profile using `ggplot2`. Values per group should be connected by a line and groups should be shown in different colors.

# Q2: Analyze the data using data summaries

We summarize the data by computing intercept and slope per mouse. This produces two values per mouse (cluster) which can then be analyzed using linear regression.

First, we convert the time variable, which is a factor to a numeric variable, assuming that each time interval shows the same effect.

```{r}
    dLongC <- dLong
    dLongC$time <- as.numeric(dLong$time)
```

If we run a linear regression, the following code extracts `intercept` and `slope` from the regression model.

```{r}
    model <- lm(tsize ~ time, dLongC)
    cfs <- coefficients(summary(model))
    print(cfs[, 'Estimate'])
    
```

Now we run linear regressions per mouse using function `by`. We add the `group` value to the result.

```{r}
    regrPerMouse <- by(dLongC, dLong$mousenr, function(data) {
        model <- lm(tsize ~ time, data)
        cfs <- coefficients(summary(model))
        return(c(cfs[, 'Estimate'], group = data$group[1]))
   })
   # create data frame as above
   dRegrPerMouse <- as.data.frame(lapply(as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, regrPerMouse)), unlist))
```

Inspect the data frame `dRegrPerMouse`. In R, column names of data frame must not contain special characters, which is why the column for the intercept is now named `X.Intercept.`.

# Q3: Perform a mixed model analysis

In R, a mixed model can be performed using function `lmer` from package `lme4`. A random effect is specified by using a bar symbol (`|`) to separate the random variable from the group variable. Starting with only a radnom intercept, we get the following model that accounts for an effect of `group` and `time`.

```{r}
    library('lme4')
    reModel <- lmer(tsize ~ group + time + (1|mousenr), dLongC)
    print(summary(reModel))
```

Interpret the variance of the random effects.

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">

  * The variance of the random intercept is 58 which is roughly a third of variance of residuals. The proportion of the total variance is 30% (`r 58.09 / (58.09 + 136.71)`).
  * The random effect therefore is non-negligible and should be kept in the  model.
</div>

# Q3: Interpret the fixed effects part of the mixed model

The function `lmer` does not automatically report P-values. We can use function `confint` to first compute confidence intervals (CIs).

```{r}
    cis <- confint(reModel, method = 'Wald')
    print(cis)
```

Report your output.

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
```
                 2.5 %   97.5 %
.sig01             NA       NA
.sigma             NA       NA
(Intercept)  35.47509 58.84406
group2      -11.23332 12.57990
time         10.44394 16.92559
```
</div>

The Wald method does not compute confidence intervals for the random effect variances (`.sig01` corresponds to the random intercept, `.sigma` corresponds to residuals).

We focus on the CIs for fixed effects.

What can you say about the significance of the effect of `group`?

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
The confidence interval does contain 0. Therefore, the effect of `group` is not statistically signficant at the alpha level of 0.05.
</div>

What can you say about the significance of the effect of `time`?

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
The confidence interval does not contain 0. Therefore, the effect of `time` is statistically signficant at the alpha level of 0.05. This means that measurement values systematically change over time, i.e. at a later time point the mean measurements are smaller or larger than at an earlier timepoint.
</div>

Calculate a P-value corresponding to the confidence interval. The following function reverses the steps to calculate a CI from a standard error. You can use it as a template (optional: try to understand the function).

```{r}
ci2se <- function(ci, alpha = .05) {
	widthStdNormal <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2);              # 1.96 for alpha = 0.05
	return((ci[, 2] - ci[, 1])/(2 * widthStdNormal))   # length of CI divided by CI-length for SE of 1
}
```

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
```{r}
    print(ci2se(cis))
```
</div>

The following function converts a CI into a P-value using the above function.

```{r}
# compute pnorm for vectors of q, mean, se in parallel
Pnorm <- function(q, mean, se)mapply(pnorm, q, mean, se)
ci2P = function(ci, alpha = .05) {
    q <- abs(ci[, 2] + ci[, 1])/2      # half the length of the CI
    se <- ci2se(ci, alpha)             # SE derived from CI
	return((1 - Pnorm(q, 0, se))*2)    # probability mass that is outside of q
}
```

Compute the P-values using the above functions and interpret the result.
**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
```{r}
    print(ci2P(cis))

```
</div>

# Q4: Analyze effect of group on the time trend

The model from Q3 allowed to analyze an effect of `group`.

What is the interpretation of this effect when you look at different time points?

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
The effect of `group` is independent of time. This implies that according to the model, if in group 2, measurements are on avarage 0.6733 higher as compared to group 1.
</div>

Is this interpreation of effect `group` compatible with what you found when analyzing data summaries?

**filline**:  
<div class="result">
The t-test comparing slopes across the groups was statistically significant which means that the assumption that group has a constant effect over time is violated.
</div>

Devise a model that can also take into account different changes over time across the groups. Specifically, allow for different slopes in the groups.

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
If one variable (`group`) modifies the effect of another variable (slope, which is represented by variable `time`), statistically, this corresponds to an interaction. In R, an interaction is written as `var1 * var2`, when `var1` and `var2` are also included as "main" effects (i.e. non-interaction terms).
</div>

Run the model.
**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
```{r}
    reModelI <- lmer(tsize ~ group * time + (1|mousenr), dLongC)
    print(summary(reModelI))
```
</div>


Calculate P-values and interpret your result. Also judge whether this model is to be preferred over the model from Q3 using the following criteria.

Models from Q3 and Q4 are nested, i.e. if we remove the interaction from model Q4, we get back to model Q3 (model Q4 is "larger" than Q3). In this scenario, if model Q4 explains the data better, i.e. there is a signficant reduction in the size of residuals, Q4 is the better model. In this course, we judge this by looking wether assoications have improved (P-values got smaller) or there are new associations (P-value < 0.05), when comparing the  larger model to the smaller one. There are statistical tests to compare models, i.e. compute a singel P-value, which go beyond the scope of this course.

A note of caution is that models can become too large. In this case, models cannot be properly fitted (computed). Indications are warnings from the fitting functions (`lm`, `lmer`), unexpectd `NA`s in result tables, or unrealistic estimates (e.g. very large values of regression coefficients, standard errors or a residual variance close to zero). In such cases, the model is too large, i.e. overfiitting the data.

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
```{r}
    cisI <- confint(reModelI, method = 'Wald')
    print(cisI)
    print(ci2P(cisI))
```

  * All fixed effects are statistically significant.
  * Groups differ significantly at baseline, accoring to this model. This is different from Q3.
  * The interaction term is statistically signficant implying that groups differ in slope.
  * `time` is statistically signficant. This means that measurements of the reference group (group 1) change over time.
  * The model from Q4 is to be preferred over Q3 for interpreting the data.
</div>

# Q5: Compare results of a linear regression with random effects model

Fist, run a linear model corresponding to the random effects model. The random inetercept corresponds to effects of facor `mousenr` and the random effect of `time` corresponds to an interaction between `mousenr` and `time` (how is the individual mouse deviating from the reference time effect?).

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
```{r}
    lmModel <- lm(tsize ~ group * time + mousenr, dLongC)
```
</div>

Extract the coefficients like in Q2.

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">
```{r}
    cfsLm <- coefficients(summary(lmModel))
    print(cfsLm)
```
</div>

Compute the estimated effect per mouse at baseline according to this model. The estimates given for the mice are given for the reference level of time, i.e. basline, and can therefore be directly taken from the regression table. Recall that the effects `mousenrX` are differences from the reference mouse (`mousenr1`) represented by the intercept. To get mean baseline values for all mice, we have to use the intercept and all effects `mousenrX`, whereby the intercept needs to be added to `mousenrX` effects.

```{r}
    effectsNames <- paste('mousenr', 2:9, sep = '') # function paste concetanates its arguments
    effMouseI <- cfsLm['(Intercept)', 'Estimate']   # extract intercept
    effMouse <- c(effMouseI, effMouseI + cfsLm[effectsNames, 'Estimate'])   # intercept, add back intercept to effects
```

The values for the random effects can be extracted from the object `reModel` using the `ranef` function.

```{r}
    res <- ranef(reModel)
```

Create two data frames with a column for the baseline effect estimates for the fixed and random effect models, respectively, so that they can be compared. Note, that for technical reasons, there are only 9 effects of mousenr in total (`mousenr10` is missing, which has to do with the fact that variable `group` is in the model). You can ignore this fact, but make sure that you only take the first 9 random effects (`effMouseRnd <- res$mousenr[1:9, '(Intercept)']`). To compare to fixed effect estimates, we subtract the mean from the latter, as random effects have mean zero (`effMouseZ <- effMouse - mean(effMouse)`). Also create a column with the mouse number. In total, your data frame should contain columns `mouse`, `fixed`, `random` (`dfBasline <- data.frame(mouse = as.factor(1:9), fixed = effMouseZ, random = effMouseRnd)`)

Here, separate rows for the fixed and random effect estimates are required. # Q6: Two random effects

To account for indivdual differences in slope across time, a second random effect can be added as follows:

```{r}
    re2Model <- lmer(tsize ~ group + time + (time|mousenr), dLongC)
    print(summary(re2Model))
```

Writing `(time|mousenr)` implies that also a random intercept is added (R always adds an intercept if not told to not to). Upon running, warnings are emitted. This model has therefore not been cleanly fitted and we use results only to illustrate concepts related to two random effects.

Interpret the variances of the random effects including the correlation. What else is striking?

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">

  * Comparison with vriance of residuals: Both variances are smaller by roughly a factor of 2 (29.8, 38.4) as comparted to the variance of the residuals (79.4).
  * Correlation of random effects: The random effects have a correlation of -1, i.e. the random intercept perfectly predicts the slope (high random intercept → low random slope). This does not seem plausible
  * There is a warning about model convergence. In principle, such models should not be interpreted unless further sensitivity analyses have been performed (out of scope of this course).
</div>

How can you determine whether `group` has an influence on the slope of the measurement?

**fillin**:  
<div class="result">

  * The current model does not allow to answer this research question
  * Influence of one variable on another corresponds to a statistical interaction
  * The new formula is `tsize ~ group + time + (time|mousenr)`
</div>

Analyze the data to answer the research question from the previous question and interpret your findings.

**fillin**:
<div class="result">
```{r}
    re3Model <- lmer(tsize ~ group * time + (time|mousenr), dLongC)
    print(summary(re3Model))
```

  * The model does not give any warnings.
  * The variance of the random intercep is now just 1/10 of the residual variance (7.2 vs 78.2). Removing the random intercept would therefore influence results only slightly.
  * Variance of the random slope is roughly 1/4 of residual variance and seems non-negligible.
  * Correlation between random effects is -0.87. This finding is compatible with a regression-to-the-mean effect
</div>
